newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai taxi firm seen ripe for strategic purchase.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai taxi firm seen ripe for strategic purchase.

text.p: Shanghai Dazhong Taxi Co Ltd's solid profits and good management are spurring speculation the company will soon become the target of a strategic share purchase, analysts said on Wednesday.
"They're very professionally managed," said an analyst at a Japanese securities firm in Hong Kong. "The nine percent rise in net profit for 1996 wasn't stellar, but they're in a low margin business."
Dazhong on Wednesday recorded a net profit of 110.006 million yuan in 1996, up 8.91 percent from 101.007 million yuan in 1995, according to international accounting standards.

The market had also expected an announcement that Shanghai Automotive Industry (Group) Corp (SAIC) would buy a 20 or 25 percent stake in Dazhong from the city government, but the news failed to materialise.
Dazhong has declined to comment on the speculation.
"I expect this news to be announced in late May or early June but it won't have a significant impact on the company," said one local analyst.

State-owned SAIC has a joint venture with Germany's Volkswagen AG to produce cars in Shanghai, and the company is also involved in a venture with General Motors Corp to manufacture medium-sized luxury sedan cars.
"I don't expect SAIC will inject any assets into Dazhong," the analyst said. "It's a long term investment for SAIC."
Analysts said the move might cause a short-term uptick in Dazhong's share price, but will have little effect on 1997 net profits except for some savings in the purchase of new cars.
The taxi company uses Santana 1000 and 2000 model cars produced by the joint venture between the SAIC and Volkswagen.
Restricted by government limits on the issue of new taxi licences, Dazhong has been forced to diversify into other areas and purchase other taxi firms to support growth, analysts said.
"The main growth (in 1996) came from investment income, like Dazhong Insurance Company and Pudong Dazhong Taxi Company," said Ban Yang, an investment analyst for ING Barings in Shanghai.
The insurance subsidiary recorded a gross profit of 70 million yuan in 1996, while Shanghai Pudong Dazhong Taxi Co Ltd registered net profit of 45.144 million yuan, company statements said.
Dazhong's foreign currency B shares and domestic currency A shares have risen in recent weeks on talk of the possible SAIC purchase and a generous bonus issue, popular with local investors.

On Wednesday, Dazhong's B shares closed at $1.710, up $0.138 from Tuesday's close. Dazhong's board of directors have proposed a 10-for-10 bonus issue based on 1996 net and capital reserves, according to its annual report.
"Local investors want the shares (from the bonus issue) because it gives them more chips to take to the table," said Bruce Richardson, chief representative for HG Asia in Shanghai.
But analysts at foreign brokerages said Dazhong looks expensive at current levels, and continued rights issues over the past three years have diluted earnings per share (EPS).

"We like the company, but over the last three years after they have announced higher earnings they issue a cash call, usually a rights issue," Richardson said. "This causes the EPS to be stable, while western fund managers want it to grow."
